issues.legal_issue: A transferee pendente lite may be refused impleadment in a suit for specific performance when the transfer or the applicant’s conduct is improper, the application is unduly delayed, or the applicant has no subsisting interest in the property.
material_facts: The suit sought specific performance of an earlier agreement to sell immovable property.

While an injunction restrained the owner from transferring the property or creating third-party rights, the owner executed agreements and sale deeds in favour of the applicants without leave of the court.
The applicants later agreed to sell the property to another company and received a substantial part of the consideration.
The applicants had knowledge of the pending suit and injunction well before applying to be joined, but did not seek impleadment until years later and gave no tangible explanation for the delay.
By the time they sought impleadment, the applicants had agreed to transfer their interest to the other company.
The applicants and the other company had suppressed the pending suit and injunction in proceedings in which they obtained orders concerning the property.
issues.conclusion: The applicants were not entitled to be impleaded as parties to the suit because their transactions were made in violation of the injunction, their conduct and delay were not bona fide, and they had no subsisting interest requiring their presence for adjudication of the specific-performance claim.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 1 Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may add a necessary or proper party in its judicial discretion; a necessary party is one without whom no effective decree can be passed, and a proper party is one whose presence enables complete and effective adjudication. In a suit for specific performance, a purchaser may be joined where the purchaser’s conduct is above board and the application is made within a reasonable time after learning of the litigation, but impleadment may be refused for contumacious conduct, a clandestine transaction, a transfer in breach of a restraint order, or undue delay. Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 makes a pendente lite transfer subject to the outcome of the litigation; it does not by itself give the transferee a right to be joined. The Court relied on Ramesh Hirachand Kundanmal v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, Anil Kumar Singh v. Shivnath Mishra, Mumbai International Airport (P) Ltd. v. Regency Convention Centre and Hotels (P) Ltd., Kasturi v. Iyyamperumal, Amit Kumar Shaw v. Farida Khatoon, Savitri Devi v. DJ, Gorakhpur, Surjit Singh v. Harbans Singh, Sarvinder Singh v. Dalip Singh, Bibi Zubaida Khatoon v. Nabi Hassan, and Vinod Seth v. Devinder Bajaj.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and (transfer_made_despite_court_restriction or clandestine_property_transaction or application_delayed_after_knowledge or applicant_has_no_subsisting_interest)

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable property.
predicates.transfer_made_despite_court_restriction: The property owner transferred or agreed to transfer the property despite a court order restricting transfers or creation of third-party rights.
predicates.clandestine_property_transaction: The applicant participated in a concealed or collusive transaction concerning the property.
predicates.application_delayed_after_knowledge: The applicant knew of the pending proceeding but waited an unreasonable time before seeking to be joined.
predicates.applicant_has_no_subsisting_interest: The applicant transferred its claimed interest in the property before seeking to be joined.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, impleadment may be refused where the applicant’s acquisition or conduct was improper, the applicant delayed applying after learning of the suit, or the applicant no longer held a subsisting interest.

issues.legal_issue: A court already dealing with a specific-performance dispute may appoint a receiver to protect the property despite a receiver appointed in a separate proceeding when the property faces a risk of further alienation and the other court has made its order subject to the first court’s directions.
material_facts: The specific-performance suit and an injunction concerning the property were pending before one court before the other company sought enforcement of an arbitral award in a separate proceeding.
A receiver was appointed in the separate proceeding and took symbolic possession of the property.
The separate proceeding and the receiver application had proceeded without disclosure of the earlier suit and injunction.

After being informed of the earlier proceedings, the court handling the separate proceeding stated that its order would be subject to orders made in the specific-performance suit and directed the decree-holder to seek appropriate orders there.

The property owner and subsequent transferees had entered into transactions in breach of the injunction, giving rise to a strong likelihood of further attempts to alienate the property if it was not protected.
issues.conclusion: The court was justified in appointing a receiver to manage and protect the property, and the appointment of a receiver in the separate proceeding did not prevent it from doing so.
issues.legal_principle: Order 40 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers a court to appoint a receiver. The Court accepted the principle, cited in Kerr on Receivers, 16th Edition, that a receiver may be appointed on an application in a specific-performance suit where a fair prima facie case for specific performance is shown; the cited authorities included C. Kennedy v. Lee, M. Cloudy v. Phelps, and Re Stephard. Judicial propriety and comity require courts to avoid conflicting orders, but the other court here had expressly made its order subject to the orders in the earlier proceeding after learning of the material facts. The earlier court’s appointment of a receiver therefore did not preclude the court already seized of the property dispute from protecting the property.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable property.
predicates.property_at_risk_of_further_alienation: The owner or transferees have engaged in transactions concerning the property that create a risk of further alienation if it is not protected.
predicates.first_court_seized_of_dispute_before_com: One court was already dealing with the dispute over the property before a receiver was appointed in a separate proceeding.
predicates.competing_court_made_order_subject_to_fi: The court in the separate proceeding stated that its order would be subject to orders made in the proceeding already dealing with the property dispute.

issues.definition: A receiver may be appointed to protect property at risk of further alienation where the court dealing with the specific-performance dispute was seized of it first and the separate court made its receiver order subject to that court’s directions.
